george.text: A passenger register records George as a painter. In Spring City, the preservation inventory associates him with house painting and carpentry. The family research reports a GD livestock brand in Sanpete County on May 24, 1876. The entry image remains to be located.

edward.text: The family account reports that Edward died during the overland journey. The manifest transcription lists an infant named Edmund Dowrard. The identification remains open.

john.text: Newspaper excerpts connect John to ranching around Woodside and Nine Mile. A published marriage-license notice places John and Minnie in Harper in 1915. The archive keeps undated land reports separate from dated life events.

minnie.name: Minnie Estelle Thompson Rogers Downard
minnie.text: The obituary reports that Minnie moved to Nine Mile with her family around age six. She had used the surname Rogers and reportedly had six children from her first marriage, three of whom survived her. The 1915 license notice names her and John as residents of Harper.
minnie.notes: The reported surviving relatives include Maud May Smith, Florence Jones, Frank Thompson, Richard Thompson, John Thompson and William E. Cassaday. Their precise relationships and spellings need checking against the original notice.

richard-thompson.name: Richard B. Thompson
richard-thompson.text: Named as Minnie’s father in the supplied obituary transcription.

alfalona-fausett.name: Alfalona Fausett Thompson
alfalona-fausett.text: Named as Minnie’s mother in the supplied obituary transcription. The reported spelling awaits corroboration.

walter.text: The September 1921 newspaper notice describes Walter as being from Price and Clace Bradley as being from Vernal. It places their wedding in Provo.

clace.text: Clace used Sabey, Bradley and Downard at different stages of her life. She married Marshall “Mack” Bradley in 1917 and Walter Downard in 1921. Oaka, Barbara and Mary Jane Bradley were Walter’s stepchildren.

thomas.text: Family information describes US Army service during World War II and later Postal Service work. The unit assignment awaits service records. The family record and newspaper summary give different dates for his wedding to Norma.

aliases: Norma Lucille Jameson Lambson (variant in supplied research)
norma.text: Norma’s 1942 marriage joined the Lambson and Downard branches. The family record gives June 26 and the supplied newspaper summary gives June 30. Robert, Glen and Quinn are listed as their children.

robert.text: Robert is part of the direct Downard line. The same-name Vernal police chief remains a separate research lead.

thomas-freestone.name: Thomas Freestone
thomas-freestone.text: Thomas and Ann appear together in the 1853 Daniel A. Miller and John W. Cooley traveling group. Family accounts connect their earlier route to Suffolk, Prince Edward Island and Iowa.

ann-fall.name: Ann Fall
ann-fall.text: Ann appears in the 1853 traveling group with Thomas and children including George, James Fall, Elizabeth Ann, Rhoda Francis, Johannah and Emma Sarah Freestone.

george-freestone.name: George Freestone
george-freestone.text: George appears in the 1853 traveling group. The county history reportedly lists a George Freestone among bishops associated with the early Uintah Stake and names a man of that name among those present at the 1888 Co-op robbery. The robbery identification remains provisional. A family history lists four children with Alice Jane Carlisle and eleven with Eraimine Georgine Lind.

alice-carlisle.name: Alice Jane Carlisle
alice-carlisle.text: Named as George Freestone’s wife in the Freestone family account.

jennie-lind.name: Eraimine Georgine Lind
jennie-lind.text: The family account identifies Jennie Lind as George Freestone’s second wife. The supplied research records their marriage in 1872.

reuben-freestone.name: Reuben Thomas Freestone
reuben-freestone.text: The family account lists Reuben among the children of George Freestone and Jennie Lind. He married Adora Elvira Batty; they were the parents of Clyde Thomas Freestone.

tom-freestone.name: Clyde Thomas Freestone

portrait.caption: Clyde Thomas “Tom” Freestone · Colorized historical photograph

tom-freestone.text: The obituary summary describes Tom as a B-17 aerial gunner who was wounded and taken prisoner after an aircraft loss near Vienna. County history reportedly records his 1964 appointment to direct juvenile court services for five eastern Utah counties. Family research also records ranching, local preservation, education and parkland donation.

maurine-peterson.name: Maurine Peterson
maurine-peterson.text: The family record identifies Maurine and Maxine as twins and records Maurine’s marriage to Tom Freestone on June 24, 1947.

maxine-peterson.name: Maxine Peterson
maxine-peterson.text: The supplied family history records Maxine as Maurine’s twin. Later life details await supporting records.

hilmer.name: Erik Hilmer Pettersson
hilmer.text: Pettersson and Peterson are spelling variants used for Hilmer. A 1959 letter describes him arriving in America as a boy. Other family records point to a later arrival. The date and ship remain unresolved.

mary-alvey.name: Mary Alvey
mary-alvey.text: Her granddaughter’s account describes Mary’s work in the family flour mills and names nine children, including the twins Maxine and Maurine.

stories.title: The Downard Journey to Utah
body: In the passenger register, George appears as Dowrard, a 40-year-old painter from England. The William Tapscott sailed from Liverpool on May 14 and reached New York on June 25, 1862. Sarah and several children appear in the same register.

The family research places them with the Horton D. Haight Company. That company left Florence, Nebraska, on August 10 and reached Salt Lake City on October 19. The family account reports that infant Edward died during the journey. The ship transcription’s infant entry reads Edmund, so the two records should be compared before the identification is settled.
The Spring City preservation inventory places George in town after immigration and associates him with carpentry and house painting.

stories.title: The House George Built
body: At 109 South 200 East in Spring City, the preservation inventory identifies a two-story house of oolitic limestone. Its hall-parlor form belongs to the town’s vernacular building tradition.

The inventory dates the house to around 1875 and describes its completion in the late 1870s. It records the sale to George’s son Joseph in 1882. The property entry separates the approximate construction date from the reported transfer.

stories.title: John Louis Downard and the Ranches of Eastern Utah
body: Three newspaper excerpts describe a ranch sale near Woodside, a move to Nine Mile, and proposed negotiations with Wade Harness. The excerpts survive without enough issue information to put them in sequence or identify the railroad section bosses named in the ranch report.

A separate abstract records a $3,600 warranty deed from W. M. Harness to J. L. Downard. The county and meridian are missing. The Burt and Wilson abstracts are listed separately because the shared section number leaves the parcels’ relationship unresolved.

stories.title: Minnie Thompson: From Nine Mile to Rochester
body: Minnie’s obituary places her birth in Elko County in 1880. It describes a move to Nine Mile when she was about six and records six children from her first marriage. A 1915 license notice names Minnie E. Rogers and John L. Downard as Harper residents.

The obituary reports that after months of illness she traveled to Rochester, Minnesota, for surgery for goiter. It describes complications and her return to Price, where she died at home. A separate report names Mayo Hospital. Her funeral was reported at the Price LDS Tabernacle and her burial at Price City Cemetery.
The supplied issue reference reads August 18. The year and exact death date remain open.

stories.title: A Wedding in 1942
body: The supplied summary of Bride-Elect Complimented describes a gathering at Mrs. T. A. Pedersen’s home, co-hosted by Mrs. Joseph Timothy. It records about 39 guests, a prize won by Mrs. Walter Downard, and a blue-and-green seersucker suit for the wedding.

The family record dates the marriage to June 26. The newspaper summary reports June 30 and identifies Bishop John A. Harter as officiant. The marriage return and the original newspaper issue are needed to resolve the difference and confirm the host’s identity.

stories.title: The Freestone Story
body: From distant beginnings to the people who made a place their own.

chapters.title: Chapter One — Before the Mountains
chapters.subtitle: Thomas Freestone. A life in England.
body: Every family story begins somewhere before anyone thinks to call it history.

For the Freestones, one of those beginnings belongs to Thomas Freestone, born in England in 1795. His life unfolded in a world that would have been almost unrecognizable to the generations that followed: a country transformed by industry, by movement, and by the growing possibility that ordinary families might someday build lives far from the places where they were born.

Thomas and Ann Fall belong to the earliest generations we can presently trace along this line. The pioneer database gives Ann’s birth year as 1812, while family records give 1814. Their names survive in the family record, even as the smaller details of their daily lives remain to be discovered.
We do not yet know enough to describe their home, their occupations, or the circumstances of their marriage with confidence. But we know something that matters: their family continued.

Their son George Freestone would carry the name into another generation. Family accounts trace the Freestones through Suffolk, Prince Edward Island, and the American Midwest. In 1853, the pioneer database records Thomas, Ann, and six children in the Daniel A. Miller and John W. Cooley wagon company.
History remembers the famous. Families remember the people who made everyone else possible.

chapters.title: Chapter Two — A Family Takes Shape
chapters.subtitle: George Freestone. The generations between.
body: The family account places George Freestone’s birth on Prince Edward Island in 1838, during the early years of Queen Victoria’s reign.
He lived long enough to see the world transformed. Railways connected distant places. Steamships shortened ocean voyages. Entire communities left Europe in search of new opportunities.
George’s own family history includes more than one marriage. Among the women connected to his life were Alice Carlisle and, later, Eraimine Georgine Lind, known as Jennie.
Jennie, born in 1855, would become the mother of Reuben Thomas Freestone.

The years separating George’s birth from Reuben’s tell a story larger than any single person. The family was moving toward a new century, and the world in which its children would grow up would look very different from the one George had known.
Yet family history is not simply a record of change. It is also a record of continuity.
Names were passed down. Children were raised. Relationships connected one generation to the next.
By the time George died in 1920, the family had entered the modern age.

chapters.title: Chapter Three — The Land and the Family
chapters.subtitle: Reuben Thomas Freestone. Building a life.
body: Reuben Thomas Freestone was born in 1888.
He would live through nearly a century of American history: the arrival of the automobile, two world wars, the Great Depression, the space age, and a world increasingly connected by technology.
But the most important events in a family history are not always the ones found in history books.
Reuben married Adora Elvira Batty, born in 1891. Together, they became the next generation in the Freestone family line.
Their son Clyde Thomas Freestone was born on November 25, 1923.

The family’s history in the American West provides an important setting for this generation. Ranching and rural life would become particularly significant in the story of Clyde Thomas, although the precise occupations and residences of Reuben and Adora still deserve further documentation.
Reuben and Adora both died in 1984.
They lived long enough to see their son return from a world war, build a family, and enter the later chapters of his own life.
Between the generations, history is carried not only in names and dates, but in the ordinary work of raising a family.

chapters.title: Chapter Four — The War Came From the Sky
chapters.subtitle: Clyde Thomas “Tom” Freestone.
body: Clyde Thomas Freestone was born on November 25, 1923.
To his family, he was Tom.
His generation came of age during the Great Depression, then entered adulthood as the Second World War changed the course of millions of lives.
The family’s summary of Tom’s obituary describes him serving as a gunner aboard a B-17 bomber.

The B-17 Flying Fortress was built to carry American aircrews deep into hostile territory. Its missions demanded long hours at altitude, in freezing conditions, with enemy aircraft and antiaircraft fire threatening the men aboard.
According to that account, Tom’s aircraft was shot down near Vienna.
He was wounded and became a prisoner of war.

The account describes an extraordinary chapter of his life. Yet it cannot fully explain what he experienced. The precise mission, the men who served alongside him, the circumstances of his capture, and his imprisonment deserve to be reconstructed from military records and his own recollections wherever available.
We should resist the temptation to invent his thoughts or words.
What we know is enough to begin.
A young man from the American West went to war in Europe. He survived the loss of his aircraft, an injury, and captivity.
And eventually, he came home.
Before he could begin the rest of his life, he had to survive a war far from it.

chapters.title: Chapter Five — The Life That Followed
chapters.subtitle: Tom and Maurine.
body: War became part of Tom Freestone’s history. It did not become the entirety of his life.
He married Maurine Peterson, born March 2, 1930.
Together they raised a family.

Tom’s postwar life included ranching, an interest in archaeology, and public service. The county history reportedly records his 1964 appointment to direct juvenile court services for five eastern Utah counties.
It was work connected to the communities of the region, and to the people who would shape its future.
Maurine brought another family history into the Freestone story: the Peterson line, with roots reaching back to Sweden.
Through their marriage, two distinct family histories became one household.
Their daughter Judy Maurine Freestone would later marry Robert T. Downard, bringing the Freestone and Downard families together in another generation.

chapters.title: Chapter Six — Two Days in April
chapters.subtitle: Tom and Maurine Freestone.
body: Clyde Thomas Freestone died on April 26, 2010.
His wife, Maurine, died two days later, on April 28.
After decades of shared family history, their deaths came remarkably close together.
The dates tell us what happened. They do not tell us how the family experienced those days, and that part of the story belongs to the people who remember them.
Tom was 86. Maurine was 80.
Their lives had reached across war and peace, changing communities, growing families, and generations of children and grandchildren.
What began with distant ancestors in England had become something much larger than a surname.
It had become a family.

chapters.title: Epilogue — What Remains
body: A family tree can show that Thomas Freestone was born in 1795, that Reuben lived nearly a century, and that Tom survived a war.
But a family story asks us to see more than the dates.
It asks us to remember that these were people whose choices, hardships, relationships, and ordinary days eventually made our own lives possible.
The Freestone story is not finished.
There are photographs still to identify, memories still to preserve, and chapters waiting to be told by the people who knew them.
And perhaps that is what makes a family history worth keeping.
It remains alive as long as someone is willing to remember.

stories.title: Tom Freestone: From Prisoner of War to a Lifetime of Service
body: Tom’s obituary, as summarized in the family research, describes a wounded B-17 gunner taken prisoner after his aircraft was shot down near Vienna. The loss date, crew, turret assignment, mission count, award and march details need military documentation.

After the war the family records describe ranching around Little Brush Creek, local archaeological and preservation work, and community education. The county history reportedly records Tom’s 1964 appointment to direct juvenile court services for five counties and his work as a referee and judge pro tempore.

stories.title: The Peterson Family’s Journey from Sweden
stories.period: Late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries
body: The family records preserve both Pettersson and Peterson for Hilmer. A 1959 letter recalls his arrival as a boy and a stay with the Anderson family before his parents arrived. Other family accounts suggest a later arrival. Swedish parish records, census entries and passenger lists remain research targets.
The family tree connects the Peterson and Freestone branches through Maurine’s marriage to Tom Freestone in 1947.
